slides.title: What is a workflow?
slides.sub: The three parts of every automation, and what happens when one runs
slides.narration: Welcome to the first lesson. In the next five minutes you will learn what a workflow is, the three parts every workflow is made of, and what actually happens when one runs. Halfway through there is a short check, so you know the first half has landed before we build on it.

slides.title: The same job, done two ways

left.label: By hand
points: Open the sheet and look for new rows
Copy the name and the email
Paste them into the sales channel
Repeat all day, and hope nothing is missed

right.label: With a workflow
points: The message is written and posted
Nobody had to look, copy or paste
It happens the same way every time

slides.narration: Start with a job you may know. At Nebula, a small coffee subscription company, every new sign-up lands as a row in a spreadsheet. Someone has to notice the new row, copy the name and email, and paste them into the sales channel. It takes a minute each time, all day long. And when that person is busy, or asleep, a lead simply waits. Now the same job with a workflow. The row arrives, and the message is posted within seconds. Nobody looked, nobody copied, and it happens the same way every single time.

slides.title: So, what is a workflow?
slides.definition: A set of steps that a computer carries out for you, in order, every time a chosen event happens.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A recipe that cooks itself: once the doorbell rings, every step is followed in the same order, with nothing skipped.

slides.narration: So here is the definition. A workflow is a set of steps that a computer carries out for you. The steps always run in the same order. And they run every time a chosen event happens, with no one pressing a button. A helpful picture is a recipe that cooks itself. The moment the doorbell rings, every step is followed, in order, with nothing skipped.

The moment the doorbell rings, every step is followed, in order, with nothing skipped.

slides.title: Every workflow has three parts

note.text: Trigger → steps → action. Every automation you will ever build has this shape.

slides.narration: Every workflow, however large, is made of the same three parts. First, a trigger: the event that starts everything. Second, the nodes in between: each one is a single step that does something with the data. Third, an action: the visible result, such as a message sent or a record saved. Trigger, steps, action. Every automation you will ever build has this shape.

Trigger, steps, action.
Every automation you will ever build has this shape.

slides.title: Part 1 — the trigger
slides.lead: A trigger listens for one kind of event. When it happens, the workflow starts.

bullets.text: A new row in a spreadsheet
A form is submitted
A time on the clock — every day at 9 AM
Another system calls in (a webhook)

aside.label: Remember
aside.text: No trigger, no run. A workflow without a trigger never starts by itself.

slides.narration: Let us take the parts one at a time. A trigger listens for one kind of event, and when that event happens, the workflow starts. The event can be a new row in a spreadsheet. It can be a form being submitted. It can be a time on the clock, such as every day at nine in the morning. Or it can be another system calling in, which is called a webhook. One rule to remember: no trigger, no run. A workflow without a trigger never starts by itself.

Or it can be another system calling in, which is called a webhook.

slides.title: Part 2 — the nodes
slides.lead: Each node does one job, then passes its result to the next node along the connection.

bullets.text: Get — read data from an app or a file
Change — rename, clean or reshape it
Decide — let some data through, stop the rest
Send — post, save or email the result

aside.label: Direction
aside.text: Data travels left to right, from one node to the next.

slides.narration: Now the nodes. Each node does exactly one job, then hands its result to the next node. Some nodes get data: they read from an app or a file. Some change data: they rename it, clean it or reshape it. Some decide: they let certain data through and stop the rest. And some send: they post, save or email the result. That last kind is the action. The lines between nodes are connections, and data always travels along them from left to right.

slides.title: What happens when it runs

note.text: One trigger event = one execution, from the first node to the last.

slides.narration: So what happens when a workflow runs? One run, from start to finish, is called an execution. The trigger fires because its event happened. The data moves to the next node, which does its job and turns green. Then the next, until the last node has finished. One trigger event means one execution. Ten new rows on ten occasions means ten executions, each one complete and separate.

slides.title: Three ways a run can go wrong
slides.lead: Knowing the parts tells you where to look when something breaks.

bullets.text: It never starts — look at the trigger
A node turns red — that step failed; read its error
Everything is green, but nothing arrived — read the last node’s output

aside.label: Worth knowing
aside.text: Green means the node ran. It does not prove the result reached anyone.

slides.narration: Knowing the three parts also tells you where to look when something breaks. If the workflow never starts, look at the trigger. If a node turns red, that step failed, and its error message says why. And the quiet one: everything is green, but nothing arrived. Then open the last node and read what it sent back. Green only means the node ran. It does not prove the result reached anyone.

slides.title: The same shape, everywhere

slides.narration: This shape is not special to Nebula. You will find it everywhere. In finance: an invoice arrives by email, the amount is read, and it is saved and finance is notified. Different tools, same three parts: a trigger, steps, and an action.

slides.title: What is an item?
slides.definition: One record travelling through the workflow: one row, one order, one ticket.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: Parcels on a conveyor belt: each parcel has a label, and each station handles one parcel at a time.

slides.narration: So here is the definition. An item is one record: one row, one order, one ticket. It carries named fields, such as first name and email. And it travels from node to node. Picture parcels on a conveyor belt, where each parcel has a label and each station handles one parcel at a time.

slides.title: A node runs once for each item

note.text: 3 items in → the node runs 3 times → 3 results out.

slides.narration: This is the idea that surprises most people. The trigger hands over three rows, so three items. The next node does not run once, it runs three times, once for each item. And the last node sends three messages. Three items in, three runs, three results out.

slides.title: Messy names in, clean names out
slides.narration: Field names straight from a spreadsheet are rarely tidy. They have spaces, capitals and punctuation, and every later node would have to spell them exactly. So early in the workflow we add one node, called Edit Fields, that renames them once. After it, every later node reads short, clean names. Tidy once, early, and the rest of the workflow gets simpler.

slides.title: Why merge at all?
slides.lead: Branches often end in the same place.

bullets.text: Every order, VIP or not, must be logged
Without a merge, the log node is built twice
With a merge, both paths share one ending

aside.label: The benefit
aside.text: One ending to maintain, instead of one per branch.

slides.narration: Why merge at all? Because branches often end in the same place, for example every order must be logged. Without a merge, you would build the log node twice, once on each branch. slides.title: What does Merge do?
slides.definition: A node with two inputs that turns them into one stream of items.

slides.narration: So what does Merge do? It has two inputs. It has one output. And it has a rule for how the two are combined. Picture two roads joining, where either the lanes simply flow into one, or the cars are paired up at a junction.

slides.title: Job 1 — Append: one after the other

slides.narration: The first job is called append. The VIP branch delivers three items. The standard branch delivers seven. Merge in append mode stacks them, one group after the other. So the log node receives all ten. Append changes nothing inside the items, it only puts them in one stream.

slides.title: Two things that go wrong
slides.lead: Both are easy to spot if you count items.

bullets.text: Merge waits for both inputs before it runs
Unmatched items vanish in a combine
Matching fails on untidy values

slides.narration: So far you have used ready-made nodes for apps such as Slack. But many systems have no ready-made node. In this lesson you will reach them anyway, through their API.

slides.title: What is an API?
slides.definition: The way one program asks another program for data, or asks it to do something.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A waiter: you do not walk into the kitchen. You give an order in the agreed form, and a plate comes back.

slides.narration: An API is how one program talks to another. You send a request. You send it to an address, called a URL. And you get a response back. Think of a waiter, because you never walk into the kitchen, you give an order in the agreed form and a plate comes back.

slides.lead: The HTTP Request node asks you for exactly these.

URL: where the request goes
Authentication: who you are
Body: the data you send, if any

aside.label: Never
aside.text: Type a password or key into the node. Store it once as a credential.

slides.narration: Every request has four parts, and the HTTP Request node asks you for each. The method says what you want, where get means read and post means create. The URL says where the request goes. Authentication says who you are. And the body carries the data you are sending, if there is any. Never type a password or a key into the node itself, but store it once as a credential.

slides.title: When things break
slides.sub: What a failure really is, and how a workflow can survive one
slides.narration: Every workflow you build will fail one day. That is not a sign of bad work, it is how connected systems behave. In this lesson you will learn to make a workflow survive failure instead of stopping.

slides.title: Two kinds of failure
slides.narration: Start by telling two kinds of failure apart. A temporary failure means the other system was busy, or the network had a hiccup. Trying again a moment later will usually work. A permanent failure means the data is wrong, or a credential has expired. Trying again will simply fail again.

slides.title: By default, one error stops everything

note.text: Item 12 failed, so items 13 to 200 were never tried.

slides.narration: Here is what happens with no protection. Two hundred items leave the trigger. They are cleaned as usual. The CRM write fails on item twelve. The whole run stops, and the last node never runs. One bad item has blocked one hundred and eighty-eight good ones.

slides.title: Setting 1: retry
slides.definition: A node setting that tries the same step again, after a short wait.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: Calling back when the line was busy: the same call, a minute later, usually gets through.

slides.narration: The first protection is a node setting called retry on fail. You choose a number of tries. You choose a wait between them. And it is the right answer for temporary failures. It is like calling back when the line was busy, because the same call a minute later usually gets through.

You choose a number of tries.
You choose a wait between them.
And it is the right answer for temporary failures.

slides.title: Setting 2: continue, and keep the failures

note.text: The good items finish. The failed ones are kept, not lost.

slides.narration: The second protection is for permanent failures. Two hundred items arrive. The CRM node is set to continue on error, and to send failures out of a separate error output. One hundred and ninety-seven items are written. Three go down the error path, to be reviewed. The good items finish, and the failed ones are kept instead of lost.

If one row has bad data, continue with an error output, so the rest are not blocked. If a credential has expired, stop and alert a person, because nothing can succeed until it is fixed. Match the response to the kind of failure.

analogy.text: A specialist you send work to: you hand over a file, they do their part, and the file comes back.

slides.narration: So what is a sub-workflow? It is a workflow that is called by another one, which we call the parent. It does one job. And it returns its result to the parent. Think of a specialist you send work to, where you hand over a file, they do their part, and the file comes back.

note.text: The parent waits, then carries on with what came back.

The sub-workflow cleans them, starting from its own special trigger. And the parent continues with the four hundred and sixty-two that came back. The parent waits, then carries on with whatever was returned.

analogy.text: A blank station on the conveyor belt: parcels arrive, you decide what happens, parcels must leave.

slides.narration: The Code node runs a few lines of JavaScript. It receives items like any other node. It runs the lines you wrote. slides.title: Files and binary data
slides.sub: PDFs, spreadsheets and attachments inside a workflow
slides.narration: So far every item has been made of fields. But real work is full of files, such as invoices, spreadsheets and photos. In this lesson you will learn how a workflow carries files, and how to get data out of them.
sentences: So far every item has been made of fields.
But real work is full of files, such as invoices, spreadsheets and photos.
In this lesson you will learn how a workflow carries files, and how to get data out of them.

slides.title: Two kinds of data in one item
slides.narration: An item can actually carry two kinds of data. The first is the kind you know, with named fields such as name, email and total. Nodes can read it directly. The second is binary data, which is a whole file such as a PDF or a photo. The file is carried along with the item, but nodes cannot read inside it.

slides.title: What is binary data?
slides.definition: A file attached to an item: carried through the workflow, but not readable as fields.

parts.text: Has a name and a type
Must be extracted to be read

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A sealed envelope clipped to a form: it goes wherever the form goes, but you must open it to read it.

slides.narration: Here is the definition. Binary data is a file that travels with the item. It has a file name and a type. And it must be extracted before its contents can be read. Picture a sealed envelope clipped to a form, which goes wherever the form goes, but must be opened to be read.

slides.title: Getting data out of a file

note.text: One file went in; 120 ordinary items came out.

slides.narration: Here is how you open the envelope. An email arrives with a spreadsheet file attached. A node called Extract from File turns the file into rows. From here on everything is familiar, so a Filter keeps the valid rows. And the orders are saved. One file went in, and one hundred and twenty ordinary items came out.

slides.title: The file nodes you will use

note.text: Extract to work with the data; convert to send it on.

slides.narration: Three nodes cover most file work. Extract from File turns a file into items, and it handles CSV, Excel and the text of a PDF. Convert to File does the opposite, turning items into a file such as a report. And the read and write nodes load or save a file. Extract when you want to work with the data, and convert when you want to send it on.

slides.title: Building a file to send

note.text: 340 items went in; one item with one file came out.

slides.narration: Now the other direction. Every Monday at eight the workflow starts. It fetches three hundred and forty sales records. Convert to File turns them into one spreadsheet file. And an email goes out with the file attached. Three hundred and forty items went in, and one item with one file came out.

slides.title: Three things that go wrong with files
slides.lead: Each has a simple check.

bullets.text: A node drops the file: check it is still attached
The wrong file type arrives: test the type first
A scanned PDF has no text to extract

aside.label: The habit
aside.text: After each node, look for the file as well as the fields.

slides.narration: Three things commonly go wrong with files. A node in the middle drops the file, so check that it is still attached. The wrong file type arrives, so test the type before extracting. And a scanned PDF is only a picture, with no text to extract. So after each node, look for the file as well as the fields.

slides.title: Files, everywhere
slides.narration: Files appear in every department. Finance extracts the text of an invoice and saves the amount and the supplier. Human resources stores an uploaded CV and notifies the recruiter. A factory converts the readings of a shift into a file and emails it to the manager.
